title: JioHotstar Goes Global: Ambani Targets Diaspora in UK, Canada, Singapore
excerpt: JioHotstar replaces Hotstar in Britain, Canada and Singapore with 160,000+ hours of content across 12 languages — but no live sports at launch, and pricing runs about ten times Indian plans.
body:
• JioHotstar, the streaming platform run by the $8.5 billion Reliance–Disney joint venture JioStar, launched outside India for the first time on Sept 2, replacing Hotstar in Britain, Canada and Singapore.
  • The launch offer: more than 160,000 hours of films, TV originals, reality shows like Bigg Boss and live Star channels across 12-plus languages — but no live sports, including the IPL, at launch, owing to existing rights deals.
  • Prices run well above Indian plans: £19.99 quarterly in the UK, CA$19.99 in Canada and SG$29.98 in Singapore — versus plans starting at ₹79 a month in India.
  • The target is the 37-million-strong Indian diaspora; India's Ministry of External Affairs data points to 4 million-plus people of Indian origin across the three launch markets. The U.S. is not part of this first wave.

India's biggest streaming platform is coming for the diaspora's TV time. JioHotstar, operated by JioStar — the $8.5 billion joint venture between Walt Disney Co. and Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries — has launched overseas for the first time, replacing Hotstar in the United Kingdom, Canada and Singapore, TechCrunch reported.

Starting September 2, Hotstar "ceases to exist" in the three markets, JioStar told TechCrunch. Existing users keep their credentials, but the old app is retired; JioHotstar is on the App Store, Google Play and connected TVs. More overseas markets are planned — though the United States, where Hotstar shut its standalone service in 2021, is not in this round.

What the launch offer looks like

The service goes live with more than 160,000 hours of entertainment, according to the company: Indian films, TV originals, Bigg Boss — now a six-language franchise — and live TV channels under the Star banner such as Star Plus, Colors, Star Vijay, Asianet, Star Jalsha and Star Pravah. Content spans 12 or more languages, including English, Hindi, Gujarati, Malayalam, Kannada and Marathi, with dubs and translations.

What's missing is the engine that drives JioHotstar's Indian audience: live sports. The IPL, the Women's Premier League, Indian national cricket fixtures, Wimbledon and the U.S. Open — all on the Indian service — are absent from the global launch. JioStar said existing content deals prevent sports from migrating at launch but did not rule out adding them later, TechCrunch reported.

"South Asian audiences have a deep connection with Indian entertainment across languages, generations and households. ... We see an opportunity to build for this broader, underserved global audience — not simply export an Indian streaming service to new markets."

— Amit Malhotra, head of international business, JioStar

The pricing math

Diaspora subscribers will pay diaspora prices. JioHotstar costs £19.99 (about $27) quarterly and £69.99 (about $95) annually in the UK; CA$19.99 (about $14) quarterly and CA$49.99 (about $36) annually in Canada; SG$29.98 (about $24) quarterly and SG$69.98 (about $55) annually in Singapore. That is roughly ten times what Indian users pay: domestic plans start at ₹79 (about $0.80) a month on mobile and top out at ₹2,199 (about $23) a year.

The pricing mirrors what Hotstar already charged abroad — JioStar is not undercutting Netflix or Amazon Prime, but charging a premium to viewers with few alternatives for Indian-language entertainment. At roughly $20 a quarter, even a single-digit conversion of the diaspora audience would deliver high-margin subscription revenue on content whose cost has largely already been paid for in India.

Why now, and what it competes with

The push follows the 2024 consolidation that formed JioStar; at the time, Hotstar and JioCinema together accounted for about 85% of India's streaming audience, TechCrunch reported. Domestically the service counts more than 500 million monthly active users — scale few platforms globally can match, but in a price-sensitive market with thin per-user revenue. The diaspora, 37 million strong and concentrated in high-income markets — about 3.2 million people of Indian origin in Canada, 1.3 million in Britain and some 483,000 in Singapore, per Indian government data — is the escape valve.

Abroad, JioHotstar enters a crowded field: Netflix, Amazon Prime Video and Disney+ all court South Asian audiences with Indian-language originals, while regional services like Zee5 already sell diaspora-focused packages. JioStar's bet is depth — a 12-language catalogue, live Star channels and AI-powered personalization. The risk is relevance: without live cricket, it is asking premium prices for entertainment diaspora households may already sample elsewhere.

What's next

Watch three things: whether JioStar cracks the sports-rights problem in each market, which countries come in the second wave — and whether the U.S., home to the largest and wealthiest slice of the diaspora, makes the cut. If the UK–Canada–Singapore launch converts, this becomes a genuine global export rather than an Indian add-on.
